stages.title: Your Workspace (before writing a single line of real code)
stages.description: You cannot learn to code without a place to write it, run it, and save it. This stage exists so every topic after it has a working environment underneath it.

stages.title: Structure: HTML
stages.description: HTML comes before CSS because you cannot style what doesn't exist yet. HTML comes before JavaScript because you cannot manipulate a DOM that hasn't been defined.

stages.title: Presentation: CSS
stages.description: CSS depends entirely on HTML existing first. Ordered internally from syntax → box model → layout → responsiveness → visual polish, since each builds on the one before.

stages.title: Behavior: JavaScript (Full Sequence, dependency-ordered)
stages.description: JavaScript comes after HTML/CSS because its most motivating use case (manipulating the page) needs a page to exist. Ordered in true dependency order — language core → functions → scope/execution → closures/this/memory → data structures → strings/numbers/dates → error handling → regex → OOP → iteration → meta-programming → modules → async → HTTP → DOM/browser → performance/security → functional patterns → architecture → algorithms → tooling/testing/debugging → engine internals/spec. Topics that could otherwise appear in more than one place (e.g. spread/rest appearing under both Functions and Advanced Operators) are merged at first occurrence.

stages.title: Adding Types: TypeScript
stages.description: TypeScript only makes sense once JavaScript is solid — it's a typed layer on top of JS, not a separate language. Intro concepts come first, then the full Mastery set from Phase 01b, each ordered so foundational type mechanics (generics, narrowing) precede the advanced techniques that combine them (conditional/mapped types, template literals).

stages.title: Data: SQL Fundamentals
stages.description: SQL is intentionally placed after the full JS/TS language stack rather than earlier — it's conceptually independent of JavaScript, and interleaving it earlier would split focus mid-language. By this point you also have enough programming maturity (data structures, objects) to map naturally onto relational concepts (tables ≈ arrays of objects, rows ≈ objects, columns ≈ keys).

stages.title: Collaboration & Code Quality
stages.description: Everything in this final stage assumes you now have real, multi-file projects worth versioning, linting, and formatting properly — HTML/CSS pages, JS/TS scripts, and SQL schemas from Stages 2–6. This is why deeper Git workflows, commit hygiene, and tooling are saved for last rather than front-loaded in Stage 1, where you had nothing substantial to collaborate on yet.

stages.title: React 18 (Foundation)
stages.description: Everything else in Phase 02 sits on top of React. Next.js is a framework around React, not a replacement for it — so React must be solid, and deep, first.

stages.title: Next.js 15 App Router (Core Framework)
stages.description: Requires all of Stage 1 — the App Router is React Server Components plus a file-system router, so nothing here works without React fundamentals, hooks, and Suspense already understood.

stages.title: App Router: Advanced Routing Features
stages.description: All topics in this stage are App Router features layered on top of Stage 2's routing model — none make sense without layouts, segments, and the caching model already understood.

stages.title: Client-Side Concerns
stages.description: Independent of the App Router internals in Stage 3 — these are client-side/browser concerns that fit better once you have real components and pages to apply them to.

stages.title: Deployment
stages.description: Deliberately last. Deployment only matters once there's a real, working app — learning Vercel configuration before pages, data fetching, and routing exist would be abstract and unmotivated.

stages.title: CSS Foundations (Beyond Phase 01's CSS3 Basics)
stages.description: Phase 01's CSS3 stage covered the box model, flexbox, grid, and responsive basics. This stage picks up where that left off — the modern CSS features that Tailwind, theming, and design-token tooling all build on.

stages.title: Tailwind CSS (Utility-First Foundation)
stages.description: Requires the cascade/@layer understanding from Stage 1 — Tailwind is built on cascade layers internally, and its config system uses CSS custom properties for theming.

stages.title: Class Composition Utilities
stages.description: These three tools exist specifically to manage Tailwind utility classes at scale — none of them are useful without Tailwind (Stage 2\\) already in place, and each builds on the previous.

stages.title: Component Libraries
stages.description: Both libraries in this stage assume Tailwind (Stage 2\\) and the class-composition utilities (Stage 3\\) are already understood — shadcn/ui in particular is built directly from both.

stages.title: Forms & Validation
stages.description: Forms are placed after component libraries (Stage 4\\) because real form UIs are typically built from shadcn/Radix inputs, not raw HTML elements — though the underlying form-state logic is library-agnostic.

stages.title: General-Purpose Utilities
stages.description: These three libraries are independent of styling and forms — placed after Stage 5 simply because they're commonly reached for while building the form/data-display logic that comes right after this phase, not because of any real dependency.

stages.title: Design Tokens & Alternative Styling Systems
stages.description: Placed last deliberately — both topics here are either an extension of concepts already covered (Style Dictionary formalizes what CSS Custom Properties \+ theming already introduced) or a full alternative to the Tailwind approach (vanilla-extract), most meaningful as a comparison once Tailwind is already second nature.

stages.title: Client State: Context's Limits, Then Zustand
stages.description: React Context was introduced generally in Phase 02\. This stage starts from where Context breaks down, then introduces the tool that fixes it.

stages.title: Server State: TanStack Query, Then tRPC
stages.description: Server state (data that lives on a server and is merely cached on the client) is a fundamentally different problem from client state (Stage 1\\) — it needs caching, revalidation, and request deduplication, which is what this stage's tools provide.

stages.title: State Machines
stages.description: Conceptually independent of Stages 1–2, but placed after both because state machines are usually reached for once you've felt the pain of complex state logic that plain useState/Zustand/useReducer can't cleanly express — that pain is easier to appreciate with Stage 1–2 experience already in hand.

stages.title: Rendering & Resilience Primitives (Applied Depth)
stages.description: React.lazy, Suspense, and createPortal were already introduced at a conceptual level in Phase 02, Stage 1\. This stage doesn't re-teach the mechanics — it applies them at real-project depth, now that Stage 2's data-fetching layer exists to make Suspense-for-data meaningful.

stages.title: Browser Observation APIs
stages.description: Independent of the state/data/rendering stages above — these are browser-native APIs for observing layout and viewport changes, placed here because their most common React use case (infinite scroll, responsive components) is more meaningful with the data-fetching layer (Stage 2\\) already available.

stages.title: Virtualization & Profiling (Capstone)
stages.description: Both topics require a real, data-populated, multi-feature app to be meaningful — placed last because they're applied to everything built in Stages 1–5, not new concepts in isolation.

stages.title: Server Runtime & Framework
stages.description: Everything in this phase runs on top of Node.js and, for routing, Express — both must be solid before anything else here makes sense.

stages.title: API Design & Hardening
stages.description: Requires Express (Stage 1\\) — REST conventions are applied through Express routes, and every hardening middleware in this stage attaches to that same Express app.

stages.title: Database Layer
stages.description: Independent of Express/Node conceptually, but placed here because a real backend needs persistence, and the API/testing layer built in Stages 1–3 is what will consume this data.

stages.title: Authentication & Token Security
stages.description: Requires the database layer (Stage 4\\) — auth needs somewhere to store users and their credentials. Internally reordered from the official list: HMAC-SHA256 moved ahead of JWT, since HS256 (HMAC-SHA256) is one of JWT's standard signing algorithms — teaching JWT first would mean explaining "the token is signed" without the mechanism underneath it.

stages.title: Unit & Component Testing
stages.description: The foundation of the testing pyramid. Requires a real app with components and logic (Phases 01–05) to have anything meaningful to test.

stages.title: Containerization
stages.description: Independent of testing/CI conceptually, but placed here because Docker images are what CI will build and what deployment (Stage 5\\) will run — this stage sits at the intersection.

stages.title: Deployment & Exit A Polish
stages.description: Deliberately last. Deployment needs a tested, containerized, CI-integrated app (Stages 1–4) to deploy. The CI badge (shields.io) is the final topic since it's a status indicator for a pipeline that must already be working.

stages.title: React Native Foundation
stages.description: Requires React (Phase 02\\) as a direct prerequisite — React Native uses the same component/hooks model, with a different rendering target (native views instead of the DOM).

stages.title: Storage & Secure Token Handling
stages.description: Requires RN fundamentals and navigation (Stage 1\\) — a real app with multiple screens is what makes persistent storage meaningful.

stages.title: Native Device Capabilities
stages.description: Requires Expo (Stage 1, Topic 2\\) — most native capabilities are exposed through Expo's SDK modules.

stages.title: Performance & Internals
stages.description: Requires a real app with lists and navigation (Stages 1–3) to have anything meaningful to profile or optimize.

stages.title: Shipping
stages.description: Deliberately last. Requires a working, tested app (Stages 1–4) and EAS Build (Stage 1, Topic 2\\) as the build pipeline that makes submission possible.

stages.title: Manual HTTP Tooling
stages.description: Requires a real API to hit (Phase 05\\) — these tools exist to inspect, test, and debug HTTP requests/responses by hand, before any documentation layer is added on top.

stages.title: API Documentation
stages.description: Requires a real, stable API (Phase 05\\) and familiarity with inspecting requests/responses (Stage 1\\) — you can't document an API accurately without having manually explored its behavior first.

stages.title: GraphQL (Alternative API Paradigm)
stages.description: Placed last deliberately. Exit B's own interview-prep checklist expects you to answer "REST vs GraphQL tradeoffs" — that comparison is only meaningful once REST (Phase 05\\) and its documentation ecosystem (Stage 2\\) are already solid. Learning GraphQL first would remove the contrast that makes it click.

stages.title: Array & String Scanning Techniques
stages.description: The simplest pattern family — each operates directly on arrays/strings using nothing but the loop and indexing fundamentals from Phase 01\. No data structure beyond an array is required.

stages.title: Linear Structures: Stack & Queue
stages.description: Both structures are prerequisites for Stage 4's traversal algorithms — DFS is naturally expressed with a stack (or recursion, which uses the call stack implicitly), BFS requires a queue. This stage must come before Stage 4\.

stages.title: Traversal: BFS, DFS, and Trees
stages.description: Directly requires the queue (Stage 3, Topic 8\\) for BFS and the stack/recursion model (Stage 3, Topic 6\\) for DFS — cannot be taught before those exist.

stages.title: Interview Meta-Skills
stages.description: Requires actual DSA competence (Stages 1–6) to be meaningful — a communication framework or system design vocabulary is empty without real problems solved to apply it to.

stages.title: Self-Hosted Caching Infrastructure
stages.description: Requires PostgreSQL and a real backend (Phase 05\\) — caching only matters once there's real query load and connection pressure to relieve.

stages.title: Hosted & Distributed Caching
stages.description: Requires Redis fundamentals (Stage 1\\) — this stage is the caching-layer parallel to Phase 05's PostgreSQL → Supabase/Neon progression: self-hosted concept first, hosted/managed alternative second.

stages.title: Transactional Email
stages.description: Independent of the caching stages above — a new capability area. Ordered so the delivery mechanism (Resend) is understood before investing in a component-based templating system (React Email) that plugs into it.

stages.title: Payments
stages.description: Placed last deliberately — the most complex and highest-stakes topic in the phase, benefiting from the caching (Stage 1–2) and reliable-delivery concepts (Stage 3\\) already in place, since payment webhooks demand exactly that kind of reliability thinking.

stages.title: Request Context & Structured Logging
stages.description: Requires a real backend (Phase 05\\) with real request traffic — logging and context tracing only matter once there's something happening to log.

stages.title: Error Tracking & Uptime
stages.description: Requires structured logging (Stage 1\\) as a complementary but distinct concept — logs answer "what happened," error tracking answers "what went wrong and who does it affect."

stages.title: Log Aggregation & Observability Platforms
stages.description: Requires structured logs to exist (Stage 1\\) — these platforms exist to collect, search, and visualize exactly that output at scale, which a single server's local log files can't do.

stages.title: Product Analytics Foundation
stages.description: A distinct concern from infrastructure monitoring (Stages 1–3) — this is about user behavior, not system health. Independent of everything above, but grouped after it since it's a separate observability axis, not a prerequisite.

stages.title: Analytics-Driven Features
stages.description: All four topics require the PostHog foundation (Stage 4\\) — none of these features exist without an analytics platform and event pipeline already in place.

stages.title: Real-Time Communication
stages.description: Ordered by mechanism complexity — each topic's limitations motivate the next. Requires a real deployed app (Phase 06\\) and backend (Phase 05\\) to build real-time features on top of.

stages.title: PostgreSQL Index Depth
stages.description: Requires Phase 05's PostgreSQL fundamentals — this stage goes deeper into exactly the index/EXPLAIN ANALYZE territory Phase 05 introduced at a basic level.

stages.title: Storage & Concurrency Internals
stages.description: The deepest topics in the phase. Ordered so MVCC comes first (it explains what VACUUM cleans up), then WAL (which read replicas directly depend on for replication), then monitoring (most useful once there's real concurrent/replicated activity to observe).

stages.title: Search
stages.description: A genuinely independent theme from Stages 1–3, ordered from PostgreSQL's built-in option (needing nothing new infrastructure-wise) to increasingly dedicated, heavyweight search engines.

stages.title: LLM API Foundations
stages.description: Requires a real backend (Phase 05\\) to call these APIs from server-side, and background/job infrastructure context (Phase 09's Redis) that Stage 4 will build on. OpenAI is placed first as the first provider learned; Anthropic follows as the second, before anything compares or routes between them.

stages.title: Embeddings & Vector Storage
stages.description: Requires OpenAI API access (Stage 1\\) for the embedding model itself, and Phase 05/11's PostgreSQL depth as the storage layer these vectors live in.

stages.title: SDK & Background Jobs
stages.description: Requires RAG (Stage 3\\) to exist as real work worth simplifying (Vercel AI SDK) and queuing (BullMQ) — introducing these tools before there's a real pipeline to apply them to would make them abstract.

stages.title: Claude-Specific Depth
stages.description: Requires the Anthropic API (Stage 1, Topic 3\\) as the foundation — these three topics are all Claude-specific behavior on top of the basic Messages API already covered.

stages.title: Structured Output & Multi-Model Routing
stages.description: Both topics require both providers (Stage 1\\) to be genuinely understood — tool calling is commonly needed across either provider, and routing is meaningless with only one model to route to.

stages.title: Cost & Governance
stages.description: Requires real multi-model usage (Stage 6\\) to have actual costs across providers worth tracking and governing — introducing cost tracking before there's real usage would have nothing to measure.

stages.title: Prompt Engineering & Evaluation
stages.description: Requires real AI features to exist (RAG from Stage 3, tool calling from Stage 6\\) — both prompt engineering and evaluation are meaningfully practiced against real, built systems, not in the abstract. Evals are placed genuinely last since you need something built before you can evaluate it.

stages.title: Client-Side Storage
stages.description: Requires Phase 02's localStorage/sessionStorage as the point of comparison — IndexedDB is what those simpler APIs can't handle: large, structured, queryable client-side data.

stages.title: Browser Rendering & Animation Internals
stages.description: A cluster of APIs concerned with how and when the browser paints — ordered from the lowest-level timing primitive (rAF) to the most advanced/niche (CSS Houdini).

stages.title: Real-Time Collaboration: The Yjs Stack
stages.description: The centerpiece of this phase, and the official curriculum's designated Build in Public moment. Requires WebSockets and WebRTC (Phase 11\\) as transport context, and IndexedDB (Stage 1\\) as a persistence context — Yjs itself is transport- and storage-agnostic, and only makes sense once you understand what it's being connected to.

stages.title: Rich Text Editors
stages.description: Moved from the official ordering — ProseMirror is taught before Tiptap, not after, since Tiptap is a wrapper built directly on top of ProseMirror. This follows the same raw-before-wrapper pattern used throughout this series.

stages.title: Load Testing
stages.description: Requires a real, deployed app (Phase 06\\) — load testing has nothing to test against before then.

stages.title: Security Threat Model & Scanning
stages.description: OWASP Top 10 is placed first in this stage deliberately — it's the threat model everything else in this stage addresses. Learning ZAP, CSP, or JWT pinning before understanding what threats they mitigate would teach tool operation without the reasoning behind it.

stages.title: Secret Management
stages.description: Ordered detection-before-prevention — establishing whether a leak has already happened (trufflehog) before setting up a mechanism to stop future ones (git-secrets), the same threat-first-then-tool logic used in Stage 2\.

stages.title: Automated Security Monitoring
stages.description: A cluster of small, lightweight tools — most are single-purpose checks that build on context established earlier in this phase.

stages.title: Compliance
stages.description: Requires the practical security measures from Stages 1–4 as context — compliance frameworks attest to controls that need to actually exist first; learning the framework before the practice would be abstract.

stages.title: Build Tools
stages.description: Foundational — everything else in this phase either analyzes what these tools produce (Stage 2\\) or measures the result of using them (Stage 3).

stages.title: Bundle Analysis
stages.description: Three tools, each attached to a different build system — ordered by which build system context you already have: Next.js (Phase 02, long since known) first, Vite (Stage 1, just learned) second, and raw Rollup (the most general-purpose, underlying both Vite's production build and usable standalone) last.

stages.title: CSS-in-JS
stages.description: An independent theme from Stages 1–3. Runtime-based libraries (styled-components, Emotion) are taught before the zero-runtime alternative (Linaria) so the tradeoff Linaria addresses — CSS-in-JS ergonomics without runtime cost — is understood as a response to a real limitation, not learned in isolation.

stages.title: Infrastructure as Code
stages.description: Terraform doesn't strictly require S3 (Stage 1), but S3 makes a concrete, already-understood resource to provision as a first real Terraform example rather than an abstract one.

stages.title: Kubernetes Core
stages.description: Requires Docker (Phase 06\\) as a direct prerequisite — Kubernetes orchestrates containers, it doesn't replace understanding what a container actually is.

stages.title: Kubernetes Ecosystem
stages.description: All three topics require core Kubernetes concepts and kubectl (Stage 3\\) already in place — each is a specialized tool or resource type layered on top of that foundation.

stages.title: Caching & Optimistic Update Patterns
stages.description: Requires Phase 09's Redis work as the caching substrate these patterns are named strategies for, and Phase 04's TanStack Query as the client-side context Optimistic Updates most commonly applies to.

stages.title: Database Concurrency Control
stages.description: Requires Phase 05's transaction fundamentals and Phase 11's MVCC deep dive — these two locking strategies are different answers to the same underlying concurrent-write problem MVCC exists to manage.

stages.title: Distributed Transactions & Messaging Resilience
stages.description: The largest cluster in the phase. Requires idempotency (Stage 2, Topic 6\\) as a hard prerequisite — every pattern here involves retries, and retries without idempotency cause duplicate side effects rather than fixing failures.

stages.title: Architectural Styles
stages.description: Both topics are broader architectural styles built from the messaging reliability patterns in Stage 3 — neither makes sense taught before Outbox and DLQ exist as the mechanisms that make them work in practice, not just in theory.

stages.title: Deployment Strategy & Resilience Validation
stages.description: Requires a real, architecturally mature system (Stages 1–5) to deploy and test — both topics are about operating and validating what's already been built, not new features in themselves.

stages.title: Decision-Making Practices
stages.description: Foundational to everything that follows in this phase — Stage 4's documentation artifacts are largely the written record of the practices introduced here.

stages.title: Engineering Process Practices
stages.description: A cluster of process disciplines, mostly independent of each other, but all downstream of having a real, deployed, monitored system (Phases 05–17) to actually apply them to.

stages.title: Documentation Artifacts: Decisions & Architecture
stages.description: These artifacts are downstream of Stage 2's practices — the folder structure and files exist to hold the output of the ADR/RFC discipline, not as independent new concepts.

stages.title: Documentation Artifacts: Operational
stages.description: Each artifact in this stage draws its actual content from a specific earlier phase's work — these are downstream summaries, not new material to learn.

stages.title: Documentation Artifacts: Product & Personal
stages.description: The two most independent artifacts in the phase — neither draws on a specific prior phase's technical content the way Stage 5's artifacts do.

stages.title: API Practice
stages.description: The only genuinely technical stage in this phase — placed first, trivial before real, as a warm-up before the career/community-focused stages that make up the rest of the phase.

stages.title: Job & Talent Platforms
stages.description: Requires a complete portfolio (effectively all of Phases 01–18) to have a profile worth putting on any of these platforms. Ordered niche-to-broad: the two India/startup-focused platforms first, LinkedIn last since its payoff specifically depends on the accumulated 17-month posting history Exit E's own description assumes already exists.

stages.title: Product Launch & Community
stages.description: Requires a genuinely complete, demo-able product — ClientSync, after 18 phases of work — to have anything worth launching or discussing.

stages.title: Technical Writing Platforms
stages.description: dev.to has already been used informally throughout nearly every Build in Public section since Phase 06 — this stage is about formal platform mastery and audience-building, not the first introduction to posting there.

Streaming responses

topics.title: text-embedding-3-small
topics.intro: Requires the OpenAI API (Stage 1, Topic 1\\) as the access mechanism — embeddings are just another API call, conceptually, but the output (a vector) is a fundamentally different kind of data than a chat completion.

bullets: What an embedding actually is — a fixed-length vector representing semantic meaning
Why "small" — the cost/dimensionality tradeoff vs larger embedding models
Cosine similarity as the standard way to compare two embeddings for semantic closeness
Batching embedding requests for efficiency

topics.title: pgvector
topics.intro: Requires embeddings (4) to have vectors worth storing, and Phase 05/11's PostgreSQL depth as the database these vectors are stored in.

bullets: The vector column type — storing embeddings directly in PostgreSQL rows alongside relational data
Distance operators — L2, cosine distance, inner product — and which matches text-embedding-3-small's intended usage
Why storing vectors in PostgreSQL (vs a dedicated vector database) is often the right call — no new infrastructure, joins with existing relational data (ties back to Phase 05's schema design)
Basic similarity search — ORDER BY embedding <=> query_vector LIMIT n

topics.title: IVFFlat Index
topics.intro: Requires pgvector (5) to exist first — this is one of two index types pgvector supports for making similarity search fast at scale.

bullets: Why a sequential scan becomes too slow for similarity search as a table grows — the same motivation as B-Tree indexes in Phase 11, applied to vectors
IVFFlat's approach — clustering vectors into lists, searching only the nearest clusters
Tuning the lists parameter — the recall/speed tradeoff
When IVFFlat needs to be rebuilt as data grows

topics.title: HNSW Index
topics.intro: Same family as IVFFlat (6) — an alternative vector index type, placed immediately after for direct comparison.

bullets: HNSW's approach — a navigable graph structure, vs IVFFlat's clustering approach

Query performance and recall — why HNSW is often preferred despite the build cost
Choosing between IVFFlat and HNSW for a given dataset size and update frequency

topics.title: RAG Pattern

When to use the raw API directly vs idb — idb covers the vast majority of real use cases

topics.title: Web Workers

topics.intro: Grouped after Workers (Stage 2\\) since both are fundamentally about communication between separate execution contexts — workers talk to the main thread, Broadcast Channel lets tabs/windows talk to each other.

topics.title: requestAnimationFrame

Canceling a scheduled frame (cancelAnimationFrame)

The timeout option — forcing execution even if the browser never reports idle time
Browser support caveats and Safari's lack of support (practical consideration)

topics.title: View Transitions API

topics.title: y-websocket
topics.intro: Directly depends on Yjs (10) and WebSockets (Phase 11\\) — one of two transport providers for syncing a Y.Doc between peers.

bullets: Setting up a y-websocket server for centralized sync
Client-side connection and automatic reconnection

topics.title: y-webrtc
topics.intro: Same category as y-websocket (11) — the second transport provider, using WebRTC (Phase 11\\) for peer-to-peer sync instead of a central relay.

bullets: Peer-to-peer document sync — no central server required for the actual data flow, only for signaling (ties directly back to Phase 11's WebRTC signaling discussion)

topics.title: y-indexeddb
topics.intro: Requires both Yjs (10) and IndexedDB (Stage 1, Topic 1\\) — this is a persistence provider, not a transport provider, storing the CRDT state locally for offline access.

bullets: Persisting a Y.Doc to IndexedDB (Stage 1) so document state survives a page reload or offline period
Combining with a transport provider (11 or 12) — local persistence and network sync are independent, composable concerns in Yjs's design
Offline-first collaborative editing — making local edits while offline, syncing automatically once a transport reconnects

topics.title: Hocuspocus
topics.intro: Requires Yjs and its transport providers (10–13) to be understood — Hocuspocus is a production-ready backend server framework built specifically around Yjs, wrapping the concepts from y-websocket (11) into something deployable.

topics.title: ProseMirror

Node views and marks — block-level content vs inline formatting

Why ProseMirror is famously powerful but low-level — most teams don't use it directly, which motivates Tiptap (16)

Collaborative editing extension — connecting Tiptap directly to Yjs (Stage 5), the practical convergence point of this entire phase: a rich text editor with live multi-cursor collaboration

topics.title: OWASP Top 10

Security Logging and Monitoring Failures — connects back to Phase 10's structured logging and Sentry work

topics.title: OWASP ZAP

Interpreting ZAP's findings — triaging real vulnerabilities against false positives
Integrating ZAP into CI (Phase 06's GitHub Actions) for continuous scanning

topics.title: Nonce-Based CSP

bullets: Content Security Policy recap from Phase 05's Helmet.js — the baseline this topic extends

Testing that a nonce-based policy actually blocks unauthorized inline scripts

topics.title: JWT Algorithm Pinning
topics.intro: A specific mitigation for an authentication vulnerability class (OWASP Top 10, 4\\) — requires Phase 05's JWT knowledge directly, since this topic is about a specific flaw in naive JWT verification.

bullets: The algorithm confusion attack — a token signed with a weaker or different algorithm than the server expects, and how naive verification code can be tricked into accepting it

Running trufflehog against your own repos (all phases so far) as a real audit, not a hypothetical exercise

Combining with Husky (a natural extension of Phase 01's Git tooling work) to enforce this automatically for every commit, not just when remembered manually

topics.title: npm audit

bullets: Running npm audit locally and interpreting severity levels

topics.intro: Same category as @next/bundle-analyzer (3), attached to Vite (Stage 1, Topic 1\\) instead of Next.js.

bullets: Same treemap visualization concept as Topic 3, applied to a Vite production build
Differences in what's typically visible — Vite's more granular chunk splitting compared to Next.js's conventions

topics.title: rollup-plugin-visualizer
topics.intro: The most general-purpose of the three — since Vite (Stage 1\\) uses Rollup for production builds, this tool can analyze the same output as vite-bundle-visualizer (4), and is also usable standalone for any Rollup-based build outside Vite entirely.

bullets: Using rollup-plugin-visualizer directly in a Rollup config (or via Vite's Rollup-compatible plugin system, Stage 1) for finer-grained control than the wrapper tools (3, 4) offer
When to reach for the underlying Rollup tool directly instead of a framework-specific wrapper — custom build setups, library bundling scenarios (ties back to tsup, Stage 1, Topic 2)

topics.title: lighthouse-ci
topics.intro: Requires Phase 06's GitHub Actions to run in as an automated CI step, and bundle-size awareness from Stage 2 as one of the contributing factors to the performance scores Lighthouse measures.

bullets: Running Lighthouse audits automatically on every PR/deploy, instead of manually checking scores in Chrome DevTools
The four Lighthouse categories — performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO — and what each actually measures
Setting budgets — failing CI (Phase 06) if a score or specific metric (e.g. bundle size, connecting back to Stage 2) regresses below a threshold
Core Web Vitals specifically — LCP, INP, CLS — and why these are the metrics that actually correlate with user-perceived performance and search ranking

topics.title: styled-components
topics.intro: The original and most widely-adopted CSS-in-JS library — foundational to this cluster.

bullets: Tagged template literals — writing actual CSS inside JavaScript, with real syntax highlighting and autocomplete support in most editors
Component-scoped styles — each styled component generates its own uniquely-scoped class, avoiding the global-namespace problem of plain CSS (Phase 03)
Dynamic styling based on props — styles that change based on component state, without manually toggling classNames (Phase 02/03's clsx/CVA approach)
Theming via ThemeProvider — a runtime theming mechanism, contrasted with Phase 03's CSS Custom Properties + next-themes approach
The runtime cost — styled-components generates and injects CSS at runtime in the browser, which is the specific tradeoff Stage 4's later topics (Linaria) exist to avoid

topics.title: Emotion
topics.intro: Same category as styled-components (7) — a very similar API, placed immediately after for direct comparison.

bullets: API parity with styled-components — tagged template literals and a similar component-scoping model
Emotion's css prop — an alternative, slightly more flexible authoring style than styled-components' component-wrapping pattern
Performance differences and bundle size comparison between the two libraries
Why teams pick one over the other in practice — largely ecosystem/preference rather than a sharp technical divide

topics.title: Linaria
topics.intro: Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS — placed last since it's the response to the specific runtime-cost tradeoff flagged in styled-components (7). Conceptually the same category as Phase 03's vanilla-extract, and framed here as a direct comparison to it, not a repeat.

bullets: The zero-runtime approach — Linaria extracts styles to static CSS files at build time, using a build-time transform rather than generating styles in the browser
CSS-in-JS authoring syntax (similar to styled-components/Emotion) with none of their runtime cost — the specific gap this fills

Direct comparison to vanilla-extract (Phase 03) — both are zero-runtime, but Linaria keeps closer syntactic similarity to styled-components/Emotion, while vanilla-extract uses a more TypeScript-native styling API
Build tooling requirements — Linaria needs its own bundler integration (ties back to Stage 1's Vite, or webpack/Next.js's build pipeline) to perform the build-time extraction
Post: skipped deliberately — build tooling changes aren't visible or interesting to an outside audience.

topics.title: AWS S3
topics.intro: The simplest standalone cloud primitive in this phase — independent of Terraform and Kubernetes, but a natural starting point since both later stages may reference it (Terraform provisioning a bucket, external-secrets pulling from AWS Secrets Manager in the same ecosystem).

bullets: Buckets and objects — S3's flat storage model, and the folder-like prefix convention that simulates a directory structure
Storage classes — Standard, Infrequent Access, Glacier, and the cost/retrieval-time tradeoff between them

Access control — bucket policies vs IAM policies vs ACLs, and why misconfigured public buckets are a persistent real-world security failure (ties back to Phase 14's OWASP Top 10, Security Misconfiguration category)
Presigned URLs — generating time-limited, credential-free access to a private object (a common pattern for direct client uploads, bypassing your own backend for large file transfer)
Common use cases: user-uploaded file storage (ties back to Phase 06b's camera capture, Phase 05's file handling), static asset hosting, backups

groups.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: Declarative infrastructure — describing the desired end state, not the steps to get there (a contrast worth making explicit against imperative scripting)
Providers — the plugin model connecting Terraform to a specific cloud (AWS, in the context of Stage 1's S3)
Resources and data sources — defining new infrastructure vs referencing existing infrastructure
State — what Terraform's state file tracks, and why it's the single most important (and most fragile) part of a Terraform setup

groups.heading: Workflow
bullets: terraform init, plan, apply, destroy — the core command cycle
Reading a plan output carefully before applying — understanding exactly what will be created, changed, or destroyed
Variables and outputs — parameterizing configurations instead of hardcoding values
Modules — reusable, composable Terraform configurations

groups.heading: State Management
bullets: Remote state — storing state in a shared backend (e.g. an S3 bucket, directly applying Stage 1's topic) instead of locally, required for any team or CI-driven workflow
State locking — preventing concurrent applies from corrupting state
Practical example: provisioning an S3 bucket (Stage 1) via Terraform as the first real, concrete resource

topics.title: Terraform Cloud
topics.intro: Directly depends on Terraform (2) — a hosted platform for running the same Terraform workflow with managed state and collaboration features.

bullets: Remote execution — running plan/apply in Terraform Cloud instead of locally, with consistent environment and credentials
Managed state storage — removing the need to hand-configure a remote backend (contrasted with Terraform's own remote state setup in Topic 2)
Team workflows — approval gates before apply, variable sets shared across configurations

topics.title: tfsec
topics.intro: Requires Terraform (2) to have configurations to scan — a security scanner for Infrastructure as Code, extending Phase 14's security-scanning theme (OWASP ZAP, npm audit) into the IaC layer specifically.

bullets: Static analysis of Terraform configs — catching misconfigurations before anything is ever applied (e.g. a publicly accessible S3 bucket, Stage 1, or an unencrypted resource)
Common findings — overly permissive IAM policies, missing encryption settings, open security groups
Integrating tfsec into CI (Phase 06's GitHub Actions) — failing a pipeline before insecure infrastructure is ever provisioned, the IaC equivalent of Phase 14's npm audit CI step

topics.title: Kubernetes
topics.intro: The largest single topic in the phase (46h official) — genuine orchestration fundamentals, not just CLI commands.

groups.heading: Core Objects
bullets: Pods — the smallest deployable unit, and why it's a pod (potentially multiple containers) rather than a single container directly
Deployments — declarative, self-healing management of a set of pod replicas
Services — stable networking identity for a set of pods whose individual IPs change constantly
ConfigMaps and Secrets — externalizing configuration and sensitive values from container images (foreshadows Stage 4's external-secrets)

groups.heading: Cluster Architecture
bullets: Control plane components — API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd (conceptual)
Nodes — where pods actually run, and the kubelet's role
Namespaces — logical partitioning within a single cluster

groups.heading: Networking & Storage
bullets: Cluster networking model — how pods communicate across nodes
Ingress — routing external HTTP(S) traffic into the cluster (a K8s-native parallel to the reverse-proxy concepts implicit in Phase 06's Render deployment)
Persistent Volumes and Persistent Volume Claims — stateful storage in an otherwise ephemeral, self-healing pod model

topics.title: kind (Kubernetes in Docker)
topics.intro: Requires both Kubernetes concepts (5) and Docker (Phase 06\\) — kind runs an entire K8s cluster inside Docker containers, the practical way to actually practice the concepts just introduced without cloud costs or complex setup.

bullets: Running a full local Kubernetes cluster using Docker as the underlying container runtime for cluster nodes themselves
Why kind exists — a lightweight alternative to Minikube or a real cloud cluster for local development and CI testing
Creating and tearing down clusters quickly for experimentation

topics.title: kubectl
topics.intro: Requires Kubernetes concepts (5) to have something to control, and kind (6) or a real cluster to actually point at.

bullets: Core commands — get, describe, apply, delete, logs, exec — for inspecting and managing every resource type from Topic 5
Applying YAML manifests — the declarative resource definitions that map directly to the objects covered in Topic 5
kubectl exec for shelling into a running pod, kubectl logs for reading container output — the K8s equivalents of Phase 06's docker exec and docker logs
Contexts and namespaces — managing access to multiple clusters/environments from one kubectl installation

topics.title: Helm
topics.intro: Requires kubectl and core K8s concepts (Stage 3\\) — Helm charts deploy the same underlying resources (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps) that Topic 5 introduced, just packaged and templated.

bullets: Charts — packaged, versioned, parameterized collections of Kubernetes manifests
Why Helm exists — deploying a complex application (many interrelated K8s resources) via a single command instead of applying many YAML files by hand with kubectl (7)
Values files — parameterizing a chart for different environments without editing the chart itself
Installing, upgrading, and rolling back releases — Helm's versioned deployment history as an advantage over raw kubectl apply

topics.title: HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler)
topics.intro: A specific Kubernetes resource type — requires core K8s concepts and kubectl (Stage 3\\) to configure and observe it in action.

bullets: How HPA automatically scales the number of pod replicas (Stage 3's Deployments) based on observed metrics — typically CPU or memory utilization
Configuring target thresholds and min/max replica bounds
Connecting this back to Phase 14's k6 load testing — HPA is the mechanism that would actually respond to the kind of traffic spikes a load test simulates
Limitations — HPA reacts to current load rather than predicting it, and cold-start time for new pods matters for how quickly it can actually help

topics.title: external-secrets
topics.intro: The most specialized, integration-heavy topic in the phase — requires core K8s and kubectl (Stage 3), and is typically installed via Helm (8), making it the natural capstone of this stage.

bullets: The problem it solves — Kubernetes Secrets (Stage 3, Topic 5) are base64-encoded, not encrypted, and typically shouldn't be the ultimate source of truth for sensitive values
Syncing secrets from an external source (AWS Secrets Manager, directly connecting back to Stage 1's AWS/S3 context) into native Kubernetes Secret objects automatically

How this ties together the entire phase — AWS as the secret's true source (Stage 1), Terraform potentially provisioning the AWS-side secret store (Stage 2), and external-secrets (installed via Helm, Topic 8) bridging it into the cluster

Where + when: LinkedIn + dev.to, at the end of this phase — infra content is specifically called out as getting strong engagement from other developers.

topics.title: Cache-Aside Caching
topics.intro: Phase 09 already introduced this pattern in practice ("check cache, miss, fetch from DB, populate cache") without naming it formally — this section gives it the formal treatment and contrasts it against the alternative strategy (Write-Through, 2).

bullets: The pattern by name — application code owns cache population, checking cache first and falling back to the source of truth on a miss
Why this is the most common caching pattern in practice — simple, cache and DB can diverge briefly, but the application controls exactly when and what to cache
Failure modes — a cache-aside system serving stale data during the window between a DB write and cache invalidation

topics.title: Write-Through Caching
topics.intro: Directly contrasted against Cache-Aside (1) — a different strategy for keeping cache and source of truth in sync.

bullets: The pattern — every write goes through the cache layer first, which then writes to the underlying store, keeping cache and DB consistent by construction
Tradeoff against cache-aside (1) — write latency increases (every write touches the cache), but read-after-write staleness risk decreases
When write-through is worth the extra write latency — read-heavy workloads where consistency matters more than write speed

topics.title: Optimistic Updates
topics.intro: Placed after the caching patterns since it's most commonly paired with a client-side cache layer — Phase 04's TanStack Query optimistic update support is the direct practical context for this pattern.

bullets: The pattern — updating the UI immediately based on an assumed-successful outcome, before the server actually confirms it
Rollback handling — reverting the optimistic UI state if the server ultimately rejects the operation (ties directly back to Phase 04's TanStack Query mutation rollback mechanics)
Why this matters for perceived performance — the user sees instant feedback even though the real round-trip hasn't completed

Risk surface — optimistic updates assuming success for operations that are actually likely to fail (e.g. anything touching Stage 2's concurrency control) can create a confusing UX when the rollback happens
Version-based conflict detection — attaching a version number (or timestamp) to a row, and rejecting a write if the version has changed since it was read
Why this is called "optimistic" — it assumes conflicts are rare and only pays the cost of detecting one when it actually happens
Implementation in Prisma (Phase 05) — a version column checked and incremented on update, application code handling the conflict when the check fails
When optimistic locking fits — low-contention scenarios where most writes don't actually collide

topics.title: Pessimistic Locking
topics.intro: Directly contrasted against Optimistic Locking (4) — the opposite assumption about how likely conflicts are.

bullets: Lock-based conflict prevention — acquiring a lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in PostgreSQL, Phase 05) before reading, preventing any other transaction from modifying the same row until the lock is released
Why this is called "pessimistic" — it assumes conflicts are common enough that preventing them upfront is cheaper than detecting and retrying them
Deadlock risk — two transactions each holding a lock the other needs, and why lock ordering discipline matters
When pessimistic locking fits — high-contention scenarios (e.g. a limited-inventory checkout flow) where optimistic locking's retry cost would be too high

topics.title: Idempotency
topics.intro: Requires both locking strategies (4, 5\\) as context for why retries happen — but its real weight is as a prerequisite for everything in Stage 3: every distributed pattern that follows depends on operations being safely repeatable.

bullets: The core property — performing the same operation multiple times has the same effect as performing it once

Why this matters for retries specifically — a network failure after a write succeeds but before the client receives confirmation is genuinely ambiguous; the client can only recover safely by retrying, and retrying safely requires idempotency

Idempotency keys — a client-generated unique identifier attached to a request, letting the server recognize and safely ignore a duplicate (direct callback to Phase 09's Razorpay webhook idempotency discussion)

Where this already showed up earlier in the curriculum without being named — Phase 09's webhook handling, and now the formal foundation for Stage 3's Saga, Outbox, and DLQ patterns, all of which assume retryable, idempotent steps

topics.title: Saga Pattern
topics.intro: Foundational to this cluster — requires idempotency (Stage 2, Topic 6\\) since each saga step must be safely retryable if it fails partway.

bullets: The problem — a business transaction spanning multiple services (no single database transaction can cover all of them, unlike Phase 05's single-database ACID transactions)
Choreography vs orchestration — services reacting to each other's events independently, vs a central coordinator directing each step
Compensating transactions — since there's no rollback across services, failure requires explicitly undoing already-completed steps in reverse
Why each step must be idempotent (Stage 2, Topic 6) — a saga coordinator retrying a step after an ambiguous failure must not cause duplicate effects

topics.title: Outbox Pattern
topics.intro: Requires Saga (7) as the context it's commonly used within, and Phase 05's transaction fundamentals directly — the outbox pattern uses a real database transaction to solve a distributed reliability problem.

bullets: The problem it solves — reliably publishing an event as a consequence of a database write, when the write and the publish can't be a single atomic operation across two different systems (the DB and the message broker)
The pattern — writing the event to an "outbox" table in the same database transaction as the actual data change, then a separate process reads and publishes from that table
Why this guarantees consistency — the event write and the data write either both commit or both roll back, since they're the same PostgreSQL transaction (Phase 05)
Common use — implementing reliable saga (7) step completion events without a distributed transaction

topics.title: Dead Letter Queue
topics.intro: Requires Saga (7) and Outbox (8) as the messaging context that would actually produce messages worth routing to a DLQ.

bullets: The pattern — after a message fails processing repeatedly (beyond a retry limit), routing it to a separate queue instead of retrying forever or silently dropping it

Why this matters operationally — a DLQ makes failures visible and inspectable instead of invisible (ties back to Phase 10's monitoring/alerting stack — a DLQ with growing depth is exactly the kind of thing worth alerting on)
Reprocessing strategy — manually or automatically retrying DLQ messages once the underlying issue (a bug, an outage) is fixed

topics.title: Circuit Breaker
topics.intro: Conceptually independent of Saga/Outbox/DLQ (7–9) but grouped in this resilience cluster — requires idempotency (Stage 2, Topic 6\\) for the retries that happen once a circuit recovers.

bullets: The pattern — tracking failures when calling an unreliable dependency, and "opening" the circuit (failing fast without even attempting the call) once a failure threshold is crossed
The three states — closed (normal operation), open (failing fast), half-open (cautiously testing if the dependency has recovered)
Why this prevents cascading failures — a struggling downstream service getting hammered with retries from every caller is often what turns a partial outage into a total one
Combining with idempotency (Stage 2, Topic 6) — once a circuit closes again, retried calls must be safe to actually retry

topics.title: Event-Driven Architecture
topics.intro: Requires Outbox (Stage 3, Topic 8\\) and DLQ (Stage 3, Topic 9\\) as the reliability mechanisms that make an event-driven system actually trustworthy in production, not just a diagram.

bullets: Services communicating via events rather than direct synchronous calls — publishers don't know or care who consumes an event
Loose coupling as the main benefit — and the corresponding cost: harder to trace a single business operation across many independently-reacting services
Event schema design and versioning — events are a long-lived contract between services, unlike an internal function signature that's easy to change
Why this style needs Stage 3's reliability patterns underneath it — an event-driven system without outbox-guaranteed publishing and DLQ-handled failures is one where events can silently go missing

topics.title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
topics.intro: Requires event-driven architecture (11) as context — CQRS is frequently paired with an event-driven system, where commands produce events and a separate read model is built from consuming them.

bullets: The core split — a write model (commands) optimized for validating and applying changes, and a separate read model (queries) optimized for how data is actually displayed/queried
Why this can outperform a single shared model — the write model doesn't need to support every query shape, and the read model can be denormalized however is fastest to read
Eventual consistency — the read model updates asynchronously as it consumes events (11) from the write side, meaning a query can briefly return stale data immediately after a write
When CQRS is worth the complexity — genuinely different read/write scaling needs or query shapes; explicitly not a default choice for most CRUD-shaped features

topics.title: Multi-Tenancy
topics.intro: Requires Phase 05's database schema design fundamentals as the foundation for tenant isolation — independent of the distributed systems cluster in Stages 3–4, but needs solid relational modeling to be meaningful.

bullets: Isolation strategies — separate databases per tenant, separate schemas per tenant, or shared schema with a tenant ID column, and the isolation/cost/operational-complexity tradeoff between them

Row-level security for shared-schema multi-tenancy — enforcing tenant isolation at the database layer itself (ties back to Phase 09's Supabase RLS discussion) rather than trusting every query to remember a WHERE tenant_id = ? clause
Connection and resource considerations — how tenant count interacts with Phase 09's PgBouncer connection pooling
Tenant-aware caching — extending Stage 1's caching patterns with tenant-scoped cache keys to avoid one tenant's cached data leaking into another's response

topics.title: Blue-Green Deployments
topics.intro: Requires Phase 06's CI/CD pipeline and Phase 16's Kubernetes/infrastructure context — a deployment strategy for whatever has been built so far.

bullets: The pattern — running two identical production environments (blue and green), deploying to the idle one, then switching traffic over once the new version is verified
Why this enables near-zero-downtime deploys and instant rollback — switching traffic back to the previous environment is immediate if something's wrong
Implementing this on Kubernetes (Phase 16) — using Service selectors or Ingress rules to control which environment receives traffic
Database migration considerations — blue-green deploys get complicated when a schema change (Phase 05) isn't backward-compatible with the environment still serving traffic

topics.title: Chaos Engineering
topics.intro: Genuinely last in the phase — chaos engineering exists to deliberately break things and verify that the resilience mechanisms built throughout Stages 2–4 (idempotency, circuit breakers, DLQs, sagas) actually work under real failure conditions, not just in theory.

bullets: The core practice — deliberately injecting failure (killing a service, adding latency, dropping network connections) into a system to verify it degrades gracefully instead of catastrophically
Starting small — chaos experiments in a staging environment before ever considering production, and with a clear hypothesis about expected behavior before running one

What a chaos experiment actually validates — does the Circuit Breaker (Stage 3, Topic 10) actually open under real failure? Does a Saga (Stage 3, Topic 7) actually compensate correctly if a step fails mid-flight? Does the DLQ (Stage 3, Topic 9) actually catch what it's supposed to?
Writing up results — documenting what was broken, what held, and what was fixed, which is directly the artifact this phase's Build in Public section and Exit ★3's portfolio checklist both call out
Post: "Why I used the Saga pattern instead of a distributed transaction" — one architectural pattern (Stage 3, Topic 7), explained simply, not the whole phase at once.
GitHub: add an ARCHITECTURE.md documenting the patterns used and why — the same documented-decisions discipline Phase 12's Exit D caution already established for this curriculum.
Where + when: dev.to, one post, end of phase.

topics.title: Changesets
topics.intro: The one genuinely technical, tool-based topic in this phase — requires Phase 15's tsup as the build step producing what Changesets actually versions and publishes.

bullets: The problem — coordinating version bumps and changelog entries across a package (or monorepo of packages) without manually tracking what changed since the last release
Adding a changeset — a small markdown file describing a change and its semver impact (patch/minor/major), committed alongside the code change itself
Consuming changesets — a release step that reads all pending changesets, bumps versions accordingly, and generates a changelog automatically
Publishing workflow — combining Changesets with Phase 15's tsup build step and Phase 06's GitHub Actions to automate the actual npm publish
This is the direct mechanism behind this phase's Build in Public goal — publishing a first real npm package
The format — context (what problem/situation prompted this), decision (what was chosen), consequences (what tradeoffs follow from it)

Why ADRs matter more than comments or memory — a decision's reasoning is often more valuable to a future reader than the decision itself, especially once circumstances have changed and someone's questioning whether the original choice still makes sense

What's actually worth writing one for — significant, hard-to-reverse decisions (Phase 12's Exit D caution about documenting pgvector vs Pinecone, Haiku vs GPT-4o is exactly ADR-shaped content), not every minor implementation choice
Retroactively writing ADRs for major decisions already made across Phases 01–17 — this phase is a natural point to catch up the backlog, not just start going forward

topics.title: RFCs (Request for Comments)
topics.intro: Requires ADR practice (2) as context — an RFC is the pre-decision version of the same discipline: proposing a change and inviting discussion before committing, whereas an ADR records a decision already made.

bullets: Structure — problem statement, proposed approach, alternatives considered, open questions for discussion
When an RFC is worth writing vs when a decision is small enough to just make and document via ADR (2) afterward
The lifecycle — an RFC that reaches consensus typically becomes the basis for one or more ADRs (2) once implemented

Solo-developer context — even without a team to actually comment on an RFC, writing one forces the same rigor of considering alternatives before committing, which matters for the kind of documented decision-making Exit ★3 (Phase 17) already flagged as a portfolio differentiator

topics.title: DORA Metrics
topics.intro: Requires Phase 06's CI/CD pipeline as the thing these metrics actually measure.

bullets: The four key metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore service
Why these specific four — they're the metrics DORA's research found actually correlate with high-performing engineering organizations, not an arbitrary dashboard

Measuring them from your own pipeline — deployment frequency and lead time are readable directly from Phase 06's GitHub Actions history; change failure rate and time to restore need incident tracking (foreshadows Topic 5 and the incidents/ artifact, Stage 4)

topics.title: Blameless Post-Mortems
topics.intro: Requires Phase 10's monitoring/Sentry stack (something to have a real incident about) and ideally Phase 14/17's chaos engineering work (deliberately-caused incidents are a safe first subject for practicing this).

bullets: The blameless framing — analyzing what happened and why the system allowed it, not who made a mistake; the practice exists because blame-oriented reviews make people hide information rather than surface it
Structure — timeline of events, root cause analysis, contributing factors, action items with owners
Using Phase 14/17's chaos engineering experiments as low-stakes practice material — you already have a real "incident" (something you deliberately broke) to write a genuine post-mortem about
Directly feeds the incidents/ documentation artifact (Stage 4)

topics.title: Technical Debt Tracking
topics.intro: Requires real accumulated project history — by Phase 18, ClientSync has enough history across 17 prior phases to have genuine, trackable debt, not hypothetical debt.

bullets: Distinguishing technical debt from "code I'd write differently today" — debt implies a deliberate or understood tradeoff, not just hindsight
A lightweight tracking format — what was deferred, why, and what the cost of leaving it unaddressed actually is
Directly feeds the TECH_DEBT.md documentation artifact (Stage 4)
Recording estimates against actuals — the only way to actually improve at estimation is comparing predictions to outcomes over time
Common estimation failure patterns — optimism bias, ignoring integration/testing time, underestimating unfamiliar work
Using this phase's own official-vs-actual hour discrepancies (flagged throughout every deep doc in this series) as a live, concrete example of estimation drift worth reflecting on
Establishing what a review is actually checking for — correctness, readability, adherence to existing patterns, not just "does it work"
Self-review discipline in a solo-developer context — reviewing your own PR with the same rigor you'd apply to someone else's, before merging

topics.title: Ramp-Up Strategy
topics.intro: Conceptually points forward to Stage 4's documentation artifacts — a ramp-up strategy is largely a curated reading path through exactly those files (ARCHITECTURE.md, DECISIONS.md, and the rest), even though it's introduced here as a practice before those artifacts are built.

bullets: What a new engineer (or a future version of yourself, returning to the project after months away) actually needs to become productive quickly
Structuring an onboarding path — which docs to read first, which parts of the codebase to explore, what NOT to worry about initially
The direct connection to Stage 4 — this practice is essentially designing the reading order for the documentation artifacts about to be built

topics.title: docs/adr/
topics.intro: The literal folder structure for storing ADRs (Stage 2, Topic 2\\) — placed first in this stage since ADRs need somewhere to live before ARCHITECTURE.md (11) can meaningfully reference them.

topics.intro: Already introduced organically in Phase 17's Build in Public section as a place to document architectural patterns used and why. This is the fuller, structured treatment — not a repeat, but likely building on a first draft that already exists.

Summarizing the major architectural patterns actually implemented (Phase 17's Saga, Outbox, CQRS, Circuit Breaker, Multi-Tenancy) with links to the specific ADRs that decided them
Keeping this document high-level — detailed reasoning belongs in the individual ADRs (10), not duplicated here

Recording what was tuned and why — connecting a specific performance fix back to the k6 result that motivated it

topics.intro: Already introduced organically in Phase 14's Build in Public section ("add a SECURITY.md and note your OWASP Top 10 checks"). This is the fuller treatment, likely extending a file that already exists in some form from Phase 14\.

stage_projects.name: Dotfiles Time Capsule
stage_projects.description: Build a personal dotfiles repository that configures your entire terminal + editor environment from scratch on a fresh machine. Includes a bootstrap.sh script that installs nvm, sets Node version, configures VS Code settings.json, keybindings, and a curated extension list via "code --install-extension", and sets up SSH key generation with a checklist prompt. Domain: developer tooling / DevOps. Why it’s real: every professional engineer eventually builds this, and you’ll actually reuse it.

stage_projects.name: New Machine, Ten Minutes
stage_projects.description: Extend the dotfiles project into a single idempotent shell script that provisions a brand-new Ubuntu/macOS machine for full-stack development in under 10 minutes — installs Git, nvm, correct Node LTS, global CLI tools (pnpm, gh CLI), configures a global .gitignore, sets up commit signing with SSH keys, and verifies everything with a self-test script that prints pass/fail per component. Why it’s real: this is what onboarding scripts at real companies look like.

stage_projects.name: Team Onboarding Kit
stage_projects.description: Package the above into a shareable CLI tool ("npx create-dev-environment") that asks interactive questions (shell preference, editor, GitHub username) and generates a personalized setup repo plus a rendered onboarding README with screenshots. Publish it as an npm package others could install. Why it’s real: this is a genuine open-source-worthy tool — portfolio-impressive because it is meta (a tool that builds tools).

stage_projects.name: Recipe Card, Zero CSS
stage_projects.description: Build a single recipe page using only semantic HTML5 (article, section, figure, time, details) — no CSS at all. It must still be readable, accessible, and make logical sense structurally. Domain: food/lifestyle.

stage_projects.name: Accessible Government Notice Board
stage_projects.description: Recreate a public notice/announcements page (like a city council site) with correct heading hierarchy, ARIA landmarks, a data table of meeting minutes using proper caption/th-scope, and a downloadable-document list using semantically correct link text (no "click here"). Must pass a Lighthouse accessibility audit at 100. Domain: civic tech.

stage_projects.name: Structured Résumé That’s Also a Sitemap
stage_projects.description: Build a résumé page using HTML microdata / Schema.org (itemscope, itemprop for Person, JobPosting history) so it’s machine-readable by search engines and could populate a rich search result. Validate with Google’s Rich Results Test. Domain: personal branding / SEO engineering.

stage_projects.name: Print-Perfect Invoice
stage_projects.description: Design an invoice that looks correct both on-screen and when printed (@media print), with page-break control, so a small business could literally print/PDF it for clients. Domain: business/finance tooling.

stage_projects.name: CSS-Only Data Dashboard Skeleton
stage_projects.description: Build a responsive analytics dashboard layout (sidebar, KPI cards, chart placeholders, table) using CSS Grid + Flexbox combined, fully responsive from 320px to 4K, with no JavaScript — including a CSS-only collapsible sidebar using the checkbox hack or :has(). Domain: SaaS/analytics.

stage_projects.name: Theatre Seat Map
stage_projects.description: Build a fully CSS-driven interactive seat-selection map (like a cinema/concert booking UI) — hover states, sold/available/selected visual states, using CSS Grid for the seat layout and pure CSS (:checked, sibling selectors) for selection logic, no JS. Domain: ticketing/events. Why it’s real: real booking sites need exactly this pattern; doing it CSS-only proves deep selector mastery.

stage_projects.name: Command-Line Expense Tracker
stage_projects.description: A Node.js CLI tool that tracks expenses in a local JSON file, using Maps/Sets for category dedup, robust try/catch with custom Error subclasses, and regex-based input validation. Domain: personal finance. Covers: language core, data structures, error handling, regex. A choose-your-own-adventure engine driven by a JSON story graph, using classes for Room/Player/Item, prototypal inheritance for enemy types, and regex command parsing ("go north", "take sword"). Domain: games/interactive fiction.

stage_projects.name: Log File Forensics Tool
stage_projects.description: A Node CLI that ingests raw server log files, uses regex to extract structured events, aggregates with Maps, and flags anomalies using custom error classes for malformed lines. Domain: SRE/observability. A mini fluent query builder (db.users.where("age").gt(18).select("name")) using Proxy to intercept property access, Reflect for meta-operations, and generators for lazy result iteration. Domain: backend tooling. Covers: prototypes, classes, iterators/generators, symbols, meta-programming, Proxy, Reflect.

stage_projects.name: Reactive State Store from Scratch
stage_projects.description: Build a tiny Redux/Zustand-like state management library using Proxy for reactivity, Symbols for private internal keys, and a plugin system using meta-programming. Ship as an npm-installable package with tests. Domain: frontend infrastructure. Why it’s real: this is literally how real state libraries are built internally.

stage_projects.name: Iterable Deck of Cards / Card Game Engine
stage_projects.description: Model a deck of cards as a custom iterable (Symbol.iterator), build a generator-based shuffle/deal system, and implement Blackjack or War fully in the terminal. Domain: games.

stage_projects.name: Weather-Aware Commute Planner
stage_projects.description: A Node script that calls a real weather API and a geocoding API concurrently using Promise.all, handles partial failures with Promise.allSettled, retries with exponential backoff, and outputs a commute recommendation. Domain: productivity/logistics. Covers: modules, event loop, async, promises, HTTP/APIs.

stage_projects.name: Rate-Limited API Aggregator
stage_projects.description: A tool that fetches data from 3+ public APIs while respecting each one’s rate limit using a hand-written async queue/throttler, with correct microtask/macrotask ordering, and caches results. Domain: data engineering.

stage_projects.name: Live Order Status Simulator
stage_projects.description: Simulate an e-commerce order pipeline (payment → packing → shipping → delivered) as async stages with realistic delays, custom event emitters, and retry logic on failure. Domain: e-commerce/logistics. A fully vanilla-JS Trello-style kanban board: native Drag and Drop API, localStorage persistence, keyboard accessibility, IntersectionObserver-based lazy rendering. Domain: productivity tools. Covers: DOM, events, forms, storage, browser APIs, observers, workers, binary data.

stage_projects.name: Client-Side Image Compressor
stage_projects.description: Users drag in images, compression/resizing happens client-side via Canvas + binary data (ArrayBuffer/Blob), the compression runs in a Web Worker so the UI never freezes, and results are downloadable — zero backend. Domain: media tooling / privacy-first apps. Why it’s real: this is how tools like Squoosh.app actually work.

stage_projects.name: Multiplayer Cursor Presence Demo
stage_projects.description: Using the BroadcastChannel API, multiple browser tabs of the "same user" see each other’s mouse cursors move in real time — groundwork for the real-time collaboration phase later in the roadmap. Domain: collaborative software.

stage_projects.name: JS Performance Profiler Playground
stage_projects.description: Build a page with 5 intentional performance bugs (memory leaks, unthrottled scroll listeners, layout thrashing, closure leaks, unbounded cache) then a fixed version, documenting before/after with Chrome DevTools Performance & Memory tabs. Domain: web performance engineering.

stage_projects.name: Functional Data Pipeline Library
stage_projects.description: Build your own functional utility library (pipe, compose, curry, memoize, immutable update helpers) from scratch, fully unit-tested, then use it to process a real CSV dataset end-to-end. Domain: data processing / dev tools. A single documented codebase implementing 8 classic design patterns (Observer, Factory, Singleton, Strategy, Decorator, Command, Module, Facade), each solving a real mini-problem, with tests and a written doc explaining when to use each. Domain: software architecture. Why it’s real: genuinely useful as a portfolio artifact demonstrating architectural maturity.

stage_projects.name: Type-Safe Config Loader
stage_projects.description: A small library that loads and validates environment-variable-based app config, using discriminated unions for different deploy environments and strict TypeScript to make invalid states unrepresentable. Domain: dev tooling.

stage_projects.name: Generic Data Table Library
stage_projects.description: Build a fully generic, reusable data-table utility (sort/filter/paginate) typed with generics so it works correctly for any row shape (DataTable<User>, DataTable<Order>) with full autocomplete and compile-time safety on column keys. Domain: frontend infrastructure.

stage_projects.name: Typed API Client Generator
stage_projects.description: Given an OpenAPI-like JSON schema, generate fully-typed TypeScript API client functions using mapped types, conditional types, and template literal types (e.g. typed route strings), plus a Zod runtime validator layer so types are enforced at compile time and runtime. Domain: API tooling / codegen. Why it’s real: this is essentially what openapi-typescript and tRPC do internally.

stage_projects.name: Library Fine Calculator, In Pure SQL
stage_projects.description: Design a normalized schema (Books, Members, Loans) and write pure SQL queries (joins, aggregates) to calculate overdue fines, most-borrowed books, and member activity reports. Domain: civic/library systems.

stage_projects.name: E-commerce Analytics Query Pack
stage_projects.description: Given a realistic multi-table e-commerce schema, write 15 real analytical queries a business would actually ask for: cohort retention, top products by margin, customers at risk of churn via window functions/RFM logic. Domain: e-commerce analytics.

stage_projects.name: Query Optimization Challenge
stage_projects.description: Given a deliberately slow, badly-indexed schema and slow queries, rewrite/optimize each (correct indexes, restructuring subqueries into joins/CTEs) and document before/after EXPLAIN plans and execution time. Domain: database performance.

stage_projects.name: Open-Source-Style Contribution Simulation
stage_projects.description: Take any earlier stage project and simulate a full open-source contribution workflow solo: feature branch, Conventional Commits, a PR description template, a CHANGELOG.md generated from commit history. Domain: OSS practice.

stage_projects.name: Team Code Quality Gate
stage_projects.description: Configure a shared ESLint + Prettier config as its own publishable npm package (@yourname/eslint-config) that multiple projects could extend, including at least one custom lint rule for a project-specific convention. Domain: engineering tooling.

stage_projects.name: Git Archaeology Report

stage_projects.name: Habit Tracker with Streaks
stage_projects.description: A single-page habit tracker using function components, hooks (useState/useEffect), controlled forms, and localStorage persistence. Domain: personal wellness.

stage_projects.name: Multi-Step Job Application Wizard
stage_projects.description: A polished multi-step form (resume upload, work history, review) using component composition patterns (compound components), error boundaries per step, and portals for a confirmation modal. Domain: HR tech / recruiting.

stage_projects.name: Concurrent Rendering Image Gallery
stage_projects.description: A masonry image gallery that uses Suspense for image loading, startTransition for non-blocking filter/search updates, and an error boundary fallback per image tile. stage_projects.name: Local Business Directory
stage_projects.description: A statically generated directory of local businesses (seeded JSON/CSV data) using file-based routing, dynamic segments, and generateStaticParams. Domain: local commerce.

stage_projects.name: Newsroom CMS Front-End
stage_projects.description: A news site pulling articles from a headless data source, mixing Server and Client Components correctly (interactive comment section as client, article body as server), using Server Actions for comment submission, and ISR for article freshness. Domain: media/publishing.

stage_projects.name: Multi-Tenant SaaS Marketing Site \+ Dashboard Shell
stage_projects.description: A realistic SaaS product shell: public marketing pages (fully static, optimized metadata/SEO), an authenticated dashboard area using middleware for route protection, Route Handlers acting as a lightweight BFF, and a caching strategy documented per route (static / ISR / dynamic). Domain: B2B SaaS.

stage_projects.name: Photo App with Modal Routes
stage_projects.description: An Instagram-style photo grid where clicking a photo opens it in a modal (intercepting routes) but a direct URL visit renders the full page — correct back/forward browser behavior included. Domain: social/media. An admin panel using parallel routes to simultaneously render independent panels (e.g., analytics + recent activity + alerts) that load and error independently, plus route groups to separate authenticated vs public layouts. Domain: internal tools/admin.

stage_projects.name: Selective Cache-Busting Content Platform

stage_projects.name: Persistent Shopping Cart

stage_projects.name: Non-Next.js SPA Router Migration Demo

stage_projects.name: Server-to-Client Hydration Demo Dashboard

stage_projects.name: Portfolio Site, Two Ways

stage_projects.name: Edge-Personalized Landing Page

stage_projects.name: Themeable Component Sandbox

stage_projects.name: Pricing Page, Pixel-Faithful

stage_projects.name: Conditional Class Playground
stage_projects.description: A small set of components (badge, alert, button) with multiple visual states driven entirely by clsx-based conditional logic. Domain: design systems.

stage_projects.name: Merge-Safe Themeable Button
stage_projects.description: A Button component that accepts a className override prop and correctly merges/overrides Tailwind classes using tailwind-merge (no visual bugs from conflicting utilities), tested against 10 tricky override cases.

stage_projects.name: CVA-Powered Component Library Core
stage_projects.description: Build 6 components (Button, Badge, Alert, Input, Card, Tag) using Class Variance Authority for variant/size/state management, with full TypeScript prop inference from the CVA config. Domain: design systems / component libraries.

stage_projects.name: Accessible Custom Select

stage_projects.name: Schema-Driven Dynamic Form Builder
stage_projects.description: A form renderer that takes a Zod schema as input and dynamically renders the correct react-hook-form-powered fields (text, number, select, date) with validation derived entirely from the schema — no hardcoded field JSX per form. stage_projects.description: A small widget showing "time until" and formatted relative dates using date-fns, correctly handling timezones. Domain: events/scheduling.

stage_projects.description: A CSV import utility that uses lodash-es for deep merging/grouping/deduplication logic on messy imported records, plus nanoid for generating stable client-side temp IDs before server save. Domain: data tooling/back-office.
